title: How do you brainstorm ideas with structure in a case interview?
description: "What could the client do?" is still a structuring question. Use buckets, not a list.
hook: You brainstorm with structure by pausing for a few seconds, choosing two or three buckets that do not overlap, filling each with two or three specific ideas, and finishing with the one you would pursue first and why. "What else could the client do?" is still a structuring question, and interviewers judge how you organise ideas as much as the ideas themselves. This guide shows the method, two worked examples and the habits that separate a strong brainstorm from a list.
body:
In this guide

  • Why a list is not enough
  • The method in four steps
  • Choosing your buckets
  • Making ideas specific
  • Worked example: coffee delivery
  • Worked example: weekday hotel rooms, with numbers
  • Strong and weak answers
  • Common mistakes
  • Practise it
  • Where to practise next

Why a list is not enough

Brainstorming questions come in two flavours: "What could explain this?" (causes) and "What could the client do?" (options). Both tempt you to say ideas in the order they occur to you. The result sounds like this: "They could do marketing, maybe a loyalty scheme, or lower prices, or open new stores, or partner with someone..."

The interviewer cannot tell from that list whether you have missed anything big, whether two ideas overlap, or which one matters. Put the same ideas into buckets and all three problems go away. Buckets show coverage, keep ideas from repeating (the MECE principle) and make your answer easy to follow and write down.

The method in four steps

1. Ask for a moment

"Could I take ten seconds to organise my thoughts?" is always acceptable. Use the time to pick buckets, not to write a long list.

2. Name two or three buckets

Say the buckets before any ideas: "I'd think about this in two buckets: getting more customers, and getting more from each customer." Two or three is enough. Five buckets with one idea each is a list in disguise.

3. Give two or three specific ideas per bucket

Go bucket by bucket. Keep one idea in reserve, because the interviewer will often ask "Anything else?"

4. Prioritise before you stop

End by saying which idea you would pursue first and why, usually on impact, cost, speed and risk. A list without a priority leaves the interviewer to do your job. If you can, add how you would test it: "I'd pilot it in five stores first."

Choosing your buckets

The best buckets come from the problem itself, such as the steps of a customer journey or the parts of a profit equation. When nothing comes, fall back on a generic split. The simple splits guide has a longer list.

SplitWorks well for
Revenue vs costAny profit question
Internal vs externalCauses of a problem; options the client controls vs needs partners for
Short term vs long termTurnarounds and action plans
Customers vs company vs competitorsOpen strategic questions (the 3Cs)
Attract, convert, retainGrowth in customers, users or members

Check that your buckets do not overlap. "Marketing" and "new customers" overlap badly, because most marketing is about new customers. "New customers" and "existing customers" do not.

Making ideas specific

"Improve marketing" is not an idea. "Send lapsed members a free-class offer in January, when people are most likely to restart" is. Specific ideas name who, what and roughly how.

One concrete example from a real company lifts an answer from good to memorable. For a question about raising revenue per customer: "Airlines did this by charging separately for checked bags and seat selection." Use one or two per case, as seasoning, and only when you are sure the example is accurate.

Worked example: coffee delivery

Prompt: a coffee chain sells through delivery apps, which take a large commission. How could it make delivery more profitable?

"I'd think about it in two buckets: making each delivery order more profitable, and moving customers to cheaper channels. On the first, we could raise menu prices on the apps, as many chains do; negotiate the commission down in return for volume; and build the delivery menu around high-margin items. On the second, we could promote click-and-collect in our own app, with loyalty points to make the switch worth it. I'd start with app pricing, because it is fast and needs no investment, and test it in one city to see how much volume we lose."

Notice the shape: buckets first, specific ideas, a clear first move, and a test.

Worked example: weekday hotel rooms, with numbers

Prompt: a city hotel is full at weekends but has empty rooms on weekdays. How could it raise weekday occupancy?

Three buckets:

  • New customers: corporate rate agreements with nearby firms, meeting and conference packages.
  • New occasions: day-use rooms, coworking passes, midweek leisure breaks.
  • Better conversion: direct-booking offers, loyalty perks, better listings on travel sites.

Then screen them on revenue potential, cost, operational fit and speed. The corporate agreement looks strongest, so size it. The illustrative numbers:

  • The deal fills 10 otherwise empty rooms a night for 200 weekdays: 10 × 200 = 2,000 room-nights.
  • At a corporate rate of $90, that is 2,000 × $90 = $180,000 of room revenue.
  • Cleaning, laundry and amenities cost about $25 per occupied room, so contribution is ($90 − $25) × 2,000 = $130,000.

Now the catch. Suppose on 20 of those nights the hotel would have sold the same 10 rooms to other guests at $150. That is 200 room-nights where the deal displaces better business, losing ($150 − $25) × 200 = $25,000 of contribution. Net gain: $130,000 − $25,000 = $105,000. Still worth doing, but with blackout dates in the contract for the busiest nights.

This is what turns a brainstorm into a recommendation: you generated several different options, then explained why one beats the others.

Strong and weak answers

Weak:

"They could advertise more, do discounts, maybe partner with companies, improve the website, add a spa..."

Strong:

"I see three buckets: new customers, new occasions and better conversion. ... Of these, I'd start with corporate agreements: they fill rooms in blocks, need little investment, and we can protect peak nights with blackout dates."

The strong version has fewer ideas, but the interviewer can see its coverage, follow its logic and hear a decision.

Common mistakes

  • Starting before you have buckets. Ten seconds of silence beats two minutes of wandering.
  • Overlapping buckets. Test each idea: could it sit in two buckets? If so, redraw them.
  • Vague ideas. Replace "improve marketing" with who, what and how.
  • Too many buckets. Two or three, each with two or three ideas, is the right size for a spoken answer.
  • No priority. Always end with your first move and the reason for it.
  • Ignoring the numbers. When you can, size the top idea, as in the hotel example. It is the fastest way to show judgement.

Practise it

Have a go at each one out loud, with a two-minute limit, before you open the answer.

1. Which opening is strongest for a brainstorm?

  • "Lots of things could help, for example..."
  • "I'd think about this in two buckets: internal and external."
  • "Let me list every idea I can think of."
Show the answer

The second. Naming buckets first shows structure and makes your ideas easy to follow. The first and third promise a list.

2. A UK university wants to attract more international students. Give your ideas in two or three buckets, then pick one to start with.

Show the answer
  • Attract: scholarships in priority countries, partnerships with schools abroad, clearer rankings and graduate-job messaging.
  • Convert: faster offers, visa and accommodation support, calls between applicants and alumni.
  • New routes in: joint programmes with overseas universities, online pathway courses.

Start with conversion: it is fast, cheap and works on students who have already applied, many of whom are lost between offer and arrival.

3. Membership at a gym chain has fallen 10% this year. What could explain it?

Show the answer

Split membership into its flows: fewer people joining or more people leaving, and within each, internal or external causes.

  • Fewer joins: internal (price rise, less marketing, poorer trial offers); external (a new low-cost gym nearby, weaker consumer spending).
  • More cancellations: internal (crowded peak hours, fewer classes, poor maintenance); external (members moving to home workouts or rivals).

First move: ask for monthly joins and cancellations by site. That single cut tells you which bucket to investigate.

Where to practise next

For the brainstorm moment inside a live case, read how to answer "What else could the client do?". Then build speed with timed prompts in the structuring drills, and try a full case with a brainstorm in it, such as Visit Al Noor (how can a Gulf state double its international tourists?).
